turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr. Ellison, come in and sit. Your daughter left a note up front, but I want to hear this from you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I am perfectly all right, in my view. Claire insisted I come. I did not fall. I slid.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): She told the desk it was twice. Tell me about the first time you slid.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That was in the kitchen, about three weeks ago. I got up from the table, my legs simply went, and I slid onto the linoleum. I did not strike my head.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the second?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Last Sunday, rising from my armchair. I sat down on the carpet, more than fell. The neighbor's boy helped me up. There was no bruise to speak of.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Were you dizzy with either of those?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I would not say that I am dizzy. I have never been given to that sort of complaint.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you are on the floor, do you black out, or lose any time?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. I stay awake. I can hear the radio straight through.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain when it happens?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Claire brought a meatloaf on Sunday. It was a kindness, though a little dry. She does worry beyond what is useful.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's good she looks in. On the chest pain, though, any pressure or tightness at all?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): None. There is no chest pain.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): And shortness of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My breathing is quite ordinary.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): On an ordinary day, when you stand up from a chair, what happens?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, if I am to be exact, the room tilts. Things go a little gray at the edges for a few seconds. I suppose one would call that dizzy. I did not mean to contradict myself earlier.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I appreciate the correction. Let me say it back. Lightheaded when you stand, vision grays for a few seconds, and twice you have slid to the floor. Did I get that right?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is right. It passes if I keep a hand on the chair.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often does that gray feeling come?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Nearly every time I stand up quickly. If I rise slowly it is milder. I have not kept a count.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any racing or skipping of the heart?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My heart does not race or skip.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nausea, sweating, a headache along with it?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No nausea and no sweating. I do get a mild headache now and then, behind the eyes, but not with the standing.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's go through medicines. What do you take for your blood pressure?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, twenty milligrams, every morning. Hydrochlorothiazide, twenty-five milligrams, in the morning as well. And amlodipine.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse read your amlodipine bottle while she had you in the chair. She read ten milligrams, once a day.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, that is not correct. I take five milligrams. An older bottle is still in the cabinet from when the dose was higher, and she must have read that. I have been on five for a long time.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I have ten from her and five from you, and I cannot tell which bottle is the current one. I will not change amlodipine today. Please bring both bottles next time.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I will. I do not wish to take the wrong one.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sleeping tablets?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. For sleep I take zolpidem, five milligrams at bedtime, and melatonin, three milligrams. I take both most nights.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most nights, not every night?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I skip the zolpidem if I have already dozed off in the chair. Otherwise, yes, bedtime. I would not call it irregular.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else, a vitamin, aspirin?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin, eighty-one milligrams, every day, for my heart, they told me. And vitamin D once a week. I cannot recall the strength of that one.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any heart attack, stroke, or diabetes in your own history?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No heart attack, no stroke, no diabetes. High blood pressure for fifteen years or more. Last spring they did an echocardiogram, and they said it was borderline. I was not given a number.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline how, the squeeze of the heart, or a valve?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I cannot say which. Borderline is the only word I kept. I am sorry not to be more precise.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had surgery?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Cataract surgery, both eyes, about six years ago. Nothing after that.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you live on your own?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I do. Claire comes three evenings a week. I managed a hardware store, and I retired at seventy. I still potter in the yard when the weather is decent.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tobacco or alcohol?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I never smoked. A glass of wine on Sunday, with Claire, and that is the whole of it.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse took pressures before I came in. Lying down, 164 over 90, pulse 72. Standing at one minute, 126 over 78, pulse 94.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Those figures fit the feeling, I must admit. I had not heard them said so plainly.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd like to listen to your chest and then stand you up for a moment, if you're willing.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course, Doctor.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heart rhythm is regular, and I hear no murmur. Lungs are clear. There is no swelling at the ankles. When you stood just now you swayed and took the table, and you told me the grayness returned.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): It did, and it left once I held on. I apologize for the unsteadiness.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need. Here is where I land. I think your pressure is dropping when you stand, orthostatic hypotension, from the blood pressure tablets stacked together. I can't fully rule out a heart rhythm problem, but nothing in the story points hard that way.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I would rather not give up all of them. The pressure is the one thing we have kept in hand.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): I agree. I am changing one tablet only. We will cut the lisinopril from twenty milligrams to ten milligrams each morning. The water pill stays, and amlodipine stays, once the dose is settled.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligrams. I expect I shall need a fresh prescription.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send it to your pharmacy today. When the ten milligram tablets arrive, stop the twenties. Do not take both.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Not both.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): I also want a blood test, a basic metabolic panel, for your kidneys and potassium, with the water pill and this change. You can have it drawn this week. It is ordered.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday morning would suit me. Shall I fast?
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to fast for this one. Anytime before the week is out is fine.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Then Thursday it is.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): At night, sit on the edge of the bed and count to twenty before you walk. Zolpidem can make that trip unsteady. Please don't drive if the gray feeling is on you.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): I seldom drive now. Claire takes me to the market. I will sit and count, as you say.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): And put both amlodipine bottles in your coat so we can settle five versus ten.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do that tonight, so it is not left to memory.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks. We will repeat the lying and standing pressures then.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. And if I should slide again before then?
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you slide again, or if you faint, or that chest pain appears, don't wait the two weeks. Come in, or go to the emergency room.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): I will not wait, in that case.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to a medicine, that you know of?
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of.
[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): The mild headache behind the eyes, is that new?
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It has been years, and it is nothing like this standing trouble. I mentioned it only to be complete.
[SEG0077] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then we will leave the headache for another day. I'll see you in two weeks, Mr. Ellison. Mind the steps on the way out.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

The patient denied blacking out or 'losing any time' during the episodes, stating he stays awake throughout.
The mild headache behind the eyes was specifically denied as being associated with standing; it is not with the standing episodes.

Amlodipine dose is recorded incompletely/wrongly: the patient stated he takes 5 mg daily and said the nurse likely read an old 10 mg bottle; the current dose is unresolved rather than simply 'once daily' without dose.
The doctor advised that the hydrochlorothiazide ('water pill') should stay unchanged.
The doctor noted he cannot fully determine which amlodipine bottle is current and therefore will not change amlodipine today until both bottles are reviewed next time.

The patient reported a prior echocardiogram last spring was described to him as 'borderline,' but he did not know whether this referred to heart squeeze/function or a valve and was not given a number.

The patient asked whether he should fast for the basic metabolic panel, and the doctor said no fasting was needed and it could be done any time before the end of the week; the patient planned Thursday morning.
